A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Kyvo and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, references, and Appendices A–F. Content can be matched despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments across four datasets, including task performance, model ablations, human evaluations, and qualitative reconstructions.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds tokenizer reconstruction-loss ablations, a SAR3D comparison, and unseen-asset decoding results.

M1.justification: The stated 3D VQ-VAE latent width changes from 256 to 128 dimensions (v1 Sec. 3.4.1/Appendix D.3; v2 Sec. 3.2.1/Appendix D.2). The 512 tokens per object, 8192-entry codebook, and four-term objective remain. Pixel-space reconstruction loss already appeared in v1's appendix; its expanded treatment is not an entirely new component.

E1.justification: V2 adds autoregressive reconstruction and rendering of unseen individual Objaverse assets using Llama (Figures 4c and 12). V1's held-out asset evaluation concerned tokenizer reconstruction, while its explicit-shape scene experiments used 20 selected assets. The four established scene datasets and core tasks remain.

E2.justification: SAR3D becomes an evaluated tokenizer comparator in v2 Table 2 and Figure 4b. V1 Figure 19's frozen-Trellis encoder–decoder control is absent from the replacement tokenizer comparisons, although Trellis scene comparisons remain. AToken is newly cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Reported tokenizer training expands from 100k steps on 5,000 assets to 200k steps on approximately 168k assets. V2 Appendix A.1 also describes training on single-render-conditioned synthetic SLATs and evaluating on SLATs from the original extraction pipeline. New asset comparisons introduce relative human-ranking evaluations; established scene protocols remain.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands tokenizer validation with a controlled comparison of no auxiliary reconstruction loss, fixed-view loss, and multiple-view loss (Table 1/Figure 4a), plus unseen-asset autoregressive decoding tests. Appendix D.2 additionally reports that increasing codebook size did not help. These extend v1's qualitative reconstruction and codebook-usage analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report the random QA baseline as 0.359 ± 0.009 over 100 runs. V2's new tokenizer comparisons report mean ranks without introducing repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: V2 adds loss-ablation mean ranks of 2.828, 1.672, and 1.500, and tokenizer ranks of 1.605 for SAR3D versus 1.395 for Kyvo. It adds unseen-asset decoding results and revises reported codebook utilization from approximately 70% to all entries. These concern new or revised experiments; matched CLEVR and real-world benchmark scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The Jaccard calculation, number-encoding equations, SLAT representation, and four-term training objective retain their mathematical form. The latent-width revision specifies the architecture; no new formal assumptions, theoretical results, proofs, or derivations appear.

C1.justification: The introduction replaces the claim of outperforming prior vision specialists with the narrower claim of handling their tasks, although Sec. 3.5 retains the existing performance comparison. The central unified-framework, four-task, and single-image reconstruction contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking reconstruction quality to pixel-space supervision, texture quality to SLATs versus triplanes, and synthetic-latent transfer to similar distributions. V1's explicit qualification that held-out tokenizer assets were seen during Trellis training is not retained for the new examples. Existing data-scarcity and instruction-following limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 specifies tokenizer batch size 8, sampling reconstruction views from 150 views, and the single-render synthetic-SLAT preparation procedure, alongside revised training quantities. Most optimizer, hardware, software, serialization, and code-access information was already supplied in v1.

R1.justification: A new 3D Tokenization paragraph cites SAR3D and AToken and positions Kyvo through compact multi-object scene encoding and token efficiency. The existing LLM, VLM, and 3D-related research positioning is largely retained.

P1.justification: Shape tokenization moves from the late extension in Sec. 3.4.1 into the central cookbook in Sec. 3.2.1, substantially restructuring the progression through representation, layouts, and scene understanding. Related-work and setup passages are condensed, application sections rewritten, and appendix implementation subsections reordered.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, adds the tokenizer training diagram and multi-panel studies, replaces the earlier tokenizer reconstruction display, and redraws the codebook-usage plot. V1 Tables 3–5 become v2 Table 5a–c, and several scene-example panels are reduced or rearranged.

improvement.justification: The controlled loss study, direct SAR3D comparison, and unseen-asset decoding examples strengthen support for the tokenizer beyond v1's mainly qualitative validation. The gain is limited by incomplete reporting of the new human evaluations and removal of the frozen-Trellis reconstruction control and training-overlap qualification. The established downstream evidence and conclusions remain largely unchanged.
